meta.title: Ch 17: Due Diligence, Investigation & Forensic Accounting — MCQ Bank
meta.description: Chapter-wise practice MCQs for Chapter 17 (Due Diligence, Investigation & Forensic Accounting).

questions.q: In a buy-side financial due diligence, the analyst's 'quality of earnings' focus is on:
o: Reported EBITDA as-is
Normalising run-rate earnings — one-offs, non-arm's-length items, policy inconsistencies, and comparability
The legal title to assets
The target's ESG ratings
questions.why: QoE adjusts the historical bridge to a defensible run-rate (non-recurring items, related-party arms-length corrections, capitalisation-policy differences, working-capital patterns) because the SPA's multiples and pegs key off it — legal/tax/operational DD sit in their parallel workstreams.
questions.trend: Repeated theme in recent ICAI exam question-patterns for this paper (AI pattern estimate — not a citation to a specific past paper question).
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — DD = the discipline of un-glamorising AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.tip: Take the numbers off their stage makeup.
mem.link: Chapter 17 — Due Diligence, Investigation & Forensic Accounting

questions.q: Which set most directly signals fraud risk in a payments cycle?
o: Round-sum payments just below authorisation limits, sequential invoice numbering from a vendor at an agent's address, and no supporting delivery documentation
All of the above only when stated in the financial statements
Vendor count exceeding the industry average
A single documented dispute with a vendor
questions.why: The pattern triad of fraud red flags: structuring under approval thresholds, shell-vendor geography, and missing substance (delivery/usage trails) — any ONE can be innocent; together they form a testable hypothesis; note that 'all of the above' traps test option design, not the concept.
questions.trend: Known trap zone: ICAI objective papers repeatedly test limits/exceptions of this rule (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — red flags are a chorus, rarely a solo AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.tip: One strange note is noise; the chord is intent.
mem.link: Chapter 17 — Due Diligence, Investigation & Forensic Accounting

questions.q: Benford's law is a forensic tool because it predicts:
o: Round-number patterns only
A logarithmic distribution of leading digits (1 leads ~30% of the time), enabling anomaly flags where fabricated numbers deviate
The total of ledger balances
Digit frequencies of sequential voucher numbers
questions.why: Benford's: leading-digit (or first two digits) distribution under natural-growth processes; manipulated/fabricated data often deviates at specific digits or round-number clusters — a risk-ranking tool, not proof; applicability requires the right data characteristics (variability, no enforced ranges).
questions.trend: No dominant past-pattern signal; included for balanced coverage (AI judgement).
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — a sieve for stories about the data, not a verdict AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.tip: Truth starts with 1 more often than people do.
mem.link: Chapter 17 — Due Diligence, Investigation & Forensic Accounting

questions.q: In a forensic/digital investigation, chain of custody matters because:
o: It encrypts the evidence
It evidences that the item examined is the same, unaltered, and uncorrupted, collected by authorised hands — without it, the evidence is inadmissible/unreliable
It is a statutory format
It replaces the need to document procedures
questions.why: Documented custody trail: collection time, handler, hash for digital, storage integrity; breaks in the chain destroy reliability regardless of the forensic finding's validity — the digital-first caveat (hash the source, work on images).
questions.trend: Core concept that appears in some avatar in most attempts under the new scheme (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Lower likelihood but possible — evidence credibility travels by paperwork, not by content Included so a low-probability surprise cannot catch you cold.

mem.tip: An unguarded exhibit is a lost exhibit, however damning.
mem.link: Chapter 17 — Due Diligence, Investigation & Forensic Accounting

questions.q: A forensic accountant begins an examination based on:
o: A client's request
Predication — a reasonable basis to believe fraud occurred
Rumour alone
An audit fee
questions.why: Predication is the professional trigger; without it there is no examination, only fishing.
questions.trend: Core concept that appears in some avatar in most attempts under the new scheme (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — the threshold question AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.tip: Investigations start with a reason, not a suspicion for sale.
mem.link: Chapter 17 — Due Diligence, Investigation & Forensic Accounting

questions.q: In digital evidence collection the auditor's first technical step is:
o: Interviewing
Imaging with hash verification of the original medium
Deleting duplicates
Backing up to the client cloud
questions.why: Preserve the original, work on copies, hash for integrity — the admissibility of everything downstream rests on it.
questions.trend: No dominant past-pattern signal; included for balanced coverage (AI judgement).
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — seal first, sift later AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.tip: A copied exhibit with the right fingerprint is proof; a loose file is a rumour.
mem.link: Chapter 17 — Due Diligence, Investigation & Forensic Accounting

questions.q: In a fraud examination, original vouchers are preferred to copies because:
o: Copies are illegal
The reliability of documents: originals can be authenticated (signatures, edits, paper trail), copies can be selected or altered
Copies are heavy
Originals are faster
questions.why: Evidence hierarchy again: original documents, examined for alteration (font mismatch, insertion spacing), carry the forensic value — the chain of custody on top of that.
questions.trend: Core concept that appears in some avatar in most attempts under the new scheme (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — touch the paper the pen touched AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.tip: A photocopy has no margin — but shows none of the edits.
mem.link: Chapter 17 — Due Diligence, Investigation & Forensic Accounting

questions.q: A fraud loss measurement that nets out what the entity would have paid anyway uses:
o: Gross receipts
Cash-out (or realistic net) method: loss = direct outflows minus the value of goods/services actually received
Statutory damages
Bank balance
questions.why: Loss = the net theft (payments minus the real services delivered) — the gross method inflates where the victim received genuine value; the method must be disclosed because the difference is the report's number.
questions.trend: No dominant past-pattern signal; included for balanced coverage (AI judgement).
questions.probWhy: Lower likelihood but possible — method names move the number more than facts do Included so a low-probability surprise cannot catch you cold.

mem.tip: Count what left, less what stayed.
mem.link: Chapter 17 — Due Diligence, Investigation & Forensic Accounting

questions.q: A payments ledger of 12,000 vouchers shows leading digit '1' in 41% of amounts. Against Benford's law the auditor concludes:
o: Roughly consistent (observed 41% vs expected 30.1%) — no Benford-based exception to chase
Any deviation is conclusive evidence of fraud
Benford applies only to sequential voucher numbers
Frequencies should be uniform (11.1% each)
questions.why: Benford expects ≈30.1% for digit 1; 41% is in the workable range → no digit-driven follow-up. Benford is a sieve, never a verdict.
questions.trend: No dominant past-pattern signal; included for balanced coverage (AI judgement).
questions.probWhy: Lower likelihood but possible — reading the test (not over-claiming it) is the exam skill Included so a low-probability surprise cannot catch you cold.

mem.tip: Benford expected first-digit frequencies: 1→30.1%, 2→17.6%, … 9→4.6%; deviations flag populations for deeper work, not proof.
mem.link: Chapter 17 — Due Diligence, Investigation & Forensic Accounting

questions.q: A payments ledger of 12,000 vouchers shows leading digit '1' in 55% of amounts. Against Benford's law the auditor concludes:
o: Any deviation is conclusive evidence of fraud
Benford applies only to sequential voucher numbers
Severe under/over-representation of 55% against 30.1% expected — a fabrication/mis-grouping flag (not proof); trace the outliers
Frequencies should be uniform (11.1% each)
questions.why: Benford expects ≈30.1% for digit 1; 55% is far outside plausible sampling noise → investigate clustering (e.g., amounts just below approval thresholds). Benford is a sieve, never a verdict.
questions.trend: No dominant past-pattern signal; included for balanced coverage (AI judgement).
questions.probWhy: Lower likelihood but possible — reading the test (not over-claiming it) is the exam skill Included so a low-probability surprise cannot catch you cold.
